title: CTS Psalms — Unit 9: Psalm 103, Count Your Blessings

blocks.en: 📖 The Book of Psalms — Unit 9: Psalm 103, Count Your Blessings
blocks.es_reference: 📖 El Libro de los Salmos — Unidad 9: Salmo 103, Cuenta Tus Bendiciones

blocks.en: Professor: Dr. Wayne Cook | Director: Dr. Ted Rogers
blocks.es_reference: Profesor: Dr. Wayne Cook | Director: Dr. Ted Rogers

blocks.en: "Bless the Lord, O my soul; and forget not all His benefits." — Psalm 103:2 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "Bendice, alma mía, a Jehová, y no olvides ninguno de sus beneficios." — Salmo 103:2 (RVG)

blocks.en: 1. Count Your Blessings
blocks.es_reference: 1. Cuenta Tus Bendiciones

blocks.en: In a revival campaign many years ago, the song leader Charles M. Alexander asked a paralyzed man, who had been wheeled down the aisle in his chair, to name his favorite hymn. The man called out for "Count Your Blessings." There was no whining and no complaining from that poor man — only a vivid, settled sense of the goodness of God. He had every earthly reason to grumble, and instead he counted his blessings. That is exactly what David does in Psalm 103.
blocks.es_reference: En una campaña de avivamiento hace muchos años, el director de canto Charles M. Alexander pidió a un hombre paralítico, a quien habían llevado por el pasillo en su silla de ruedas, que nombrara su himno favorito. El hombre pidió "Cuenta tus bendiciones." No hubo queja ni lamento de aquel pobre hombre — solo un vivo y firme sentido de la bondad de Dios. Tenía toda razón terrenal para quejarse, y en cambio contó sus bendiciones. Eso es exactamente lo que hace David en el Salmo 103.

blocks.en: The old hymn says, "Count your blessings, name them one by one, and it will surprise you what the Lord hath done." David sat down to do just that — to count up all the benefits of God. The only trouble was that there were so many of them he had to tie them into bundles to remember them all, and then he shaped the bundles into a song. If more of us as Christians would praise God for His blessings and stop complaining and feeling sorry for ourselves, we would be far happier, and we could turn the world upside down. It is a tragic thing to see ungrateful, complaining Christians advertising the good news of Jesus Christ — like starving men hired to carry signs for the finest restaurant in town. It is time we counted our blessings instead of our anxieties.
blocks.es_reference: El viejo himno dice: "Cuenta tus bendiciones, una a una cuenta, y verás, sorprendido, lo que Dios por ti hará." David se sentó a hacer precisamente eso — a contar todos los beneficios de Dios. El único problema fue que había tantos que tuvo que atarlos en haces para recordarlos todos, y luego dio forma de canción a esos haces. Si más de nosotros como cristianos alabáramos a Dios por Sus bendiciones y dejáramos de quejarnos y de sentir lástima de nosotros mismos, seríamos mucho más felices, y podríamos poner el mundo de cabeza. Es algo trágico ver a cristianos ingratos y quejumbrosos anunciando las buenas nuevas de Jesucristo — como hombres hambrientos contratados para cargar carteles del mejor restaurante de la ciudad. Es hora de que contemos nuestras bendiciones en lugar de nuestras ansiedades.

blocks.en: Psalm 103:1-2 (NKJV): "Bless the LORD, O my soul; and all that is within me, bless His holy name! Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all His benefits."
blocks.es_reference: Salmo 103:1-2 (RVG): "Bendice, alma mía, a Jehová; y bendiga todo mi ser su santo nombre. Bendice, alma mía, a Jehová, y no olvides ninguno de sus beneficios."

blocks.en: 2. The First Blessing: He Forgives Our Sins
blocks.es_reference: 2. La Primera Bendición: Él Perdona Nuestros Pecados

blocks.en: The first benefit David names is forgiveness: "who forgives all your iniquities." All through the Bible, sin is pictured as a disease — a terrible disease that is always fatal, and every one of us carries it. As Romans 3:23 says, "all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God." The disease is fatal, but there is one cure: Jesus died on the cross to forgive our sins. No matter what they are, they can be forgiven; we are given a second chance.
blocks.es_reference: El primer beneficio que David nombra es el perdón: "Él es quien perdona todas tus iniquidades." Por toda la Biblia, el pecado se presenta como una enfermedad — una enfermedad terrible que siempre es mortal, y cada uno de nosotros la lleva. Como dice Romanos 3:23: "por cuanto todos pecaron, y están destituidos de la gloria de Dios." La enfermedad es mortal, pero hay una sola cura: Jesús murió en la cruz para perdonar nuestros pecados. No importa cuáles sean, pueden ser perdonados; se nos da una segunda oportunidad.

blocks.en: Think of the woman caught in her sin and dragged before Jesus, whom the crowd was ready to stone. He did not excuse what she had done, but neither did He condemn her; He said, "Neither do I condemn you; go and sin no more." That is the wonder of this first blessing. The guilt that would have crushed us, the record that stood against us, God has dealt with at the cross. When we count our blessings, this is where the counting must begin — not with health or wealth, but with a forgiven soul.
blocks.es_reference: Piense en la mujer sorprendida en su pecado y arrastrada ante Jesús, a quien la multitud estaba lista para apedrear. Él no excusó lo que ella había hecho, pero tampoco la condenó; dijo: "Ni yo te condeno; vete, y no peques más." Esa es la maravilla de esta primera bendición. La culpa que nos habría aplastado, el registro que estaba contra nosotros, Dios lo ha tratado en la cruz. Cuando contamos nuestras bendiciones, aquí debe comenzar la cuenta — no con la salud ni con la riqueza, sino con un alma perdonada.

blocks.en: 3. The Second Blessing: He Heals Our Diseases
blocks.es_reference: 3. La Segunda Bendición: Él Sana Nuestras Enfermedades

blocks.en: The second benefit is healing: "who heals all your diseases." Only a person who has suffered a severe illness and recovered can fully appreciate the gift of health. Apparently the psalmist had passed through some terrible sickness that had wrecked his body and crushed his spirit, and now that he was well again he could not stop praising God for it.
blocks.es_reference: El segundo beneficio es la sanidad: "Él es quien sana todas tus dolencias." Solo quien ha sufrido una enfermedad grave y se ha recuperado puede apreciar plenamente el don de la salud. Al parecer el salmista había pasado por alguna enfermedad terrible que había arruinado su cuerpo y aplastado su espíritu, y ahora que estaba bien de nuevo no podía dejar de alabar a Dios por ello.

blocks.en: I thank God for every instrument of healing He has given us — the doctors, the nurses, the medicines, the hospitals, all the miracles of modern medicine. But I am convinced that all healing is finally divine healing and a gift from God. The doctors do all they can do, and then we depend on God to bring the healing. Remember the woman who had been bleeding for twelve years. She had gone from doctor to doctor and spent everything she had, with no cure. Then one day she met the Great Physician, Jesus Christ, reached out and touched the hem of His garment, and was healed at once. Power flowed from Jesus, and He said to her, "Daughter, be of good cheer; your faith has made you well." Whether He heals through a physician's hands or by His own direct mercy, the healing is His gift, and it is cause to bless His name.
blocks.es_reference: Doy gracias a Dios por cada instrumento de sanidad que nos ha dado — los médicos, las enfermeras, las medicinas, los hospitales, todos los milagros de la medicina moderna. Pero estoy convencido de que toda sanidad es al fin sanidad divina y un don de Dios. Los médicos hacen todo lo que pueden, y luego dependemos de Dios para que traiga la sanidad. Recuerde a la mujer que había sangrado por doce años. Había ido de médico en médico y gastado todo lo que tenía, sin cura. Entonces un día se encontró con el Gran Médico, Jesucristo, extendió la mano y tocó el borde de Su manto, y fue sanada al instante. Poder fluyó de Jesús, y Él le dijo: "Hija, ten ánimo; tu fe te ha sanado." Ya sea que sane por las manos de un médico o por Su propia misericordia directa, la sanidad es Su don, y es motivo para bendecir Su nombre.

blocks.en: 4. The Third Blessing: He Redeems Us from the Pit
blocks.es_reference: 4. La Tercera Bendición: Él Nos Rescata del Hoyo

blocks.en: The third benefit is rescue: "who redeems your life from destruction" — literally, from the pit. The word "pit" may point to the grave and to death itself; there may have been a dark moment when the psalmist's life hung in the balance, and God reached down and pulled him back. But there is also a deeper pit in view — the eternal pit that Jesus called hell. People sometimes say lightly to one another, "Go to hell," but hell is no light matter, and we would not wish it on anyone. The great blessing of the gospel is that those who have trusted in Jesus will never be cast into that everlasting pit.
blocks.es_reference: El tercer beneficio es el rescate: "Él es quien rescata del hoyo tu vida" — literalmente, de la fosa. La palabra "hoyo" puede señalar la tumba y la muerte misma; pudo haber un momento oscuro en que la vida del salmista pendía de un hilo, y Dios extendió la mano y lo sacó. Pero también hay un hoyo más profundo a la vista — el hoyo eterno que Jesús llamó infierno. La gente a veces se dice a la ligera "vete al infierno," pero el infierno no es cosa ligera, y no se lo desearíamos a nadie. La gran bendición del evangelio es que los que han confiado en Jesús nunca serán echados en aquel hoyo eterno.

blocks.en: Saved from the Pit: A young preacher was conducting a revival service when a well-dressed woman came down the aisle and received Christ. She went home to her husband, a big, raw-boned farmer over six feet tall, and said, "Dave, I heard a young fellow preach today, and I was saved. I'm so happy — I've been worried about where I would spend eternity, and today I got saved." Her husband loved her, but he was so furious he nearly struck her. "What kind of home are we going to have," he demanded, "with you saved and me lost?" He decided to deal with that preacher the next day. He came to the service ready for a fight, and sat there as meek as a lamb instead. He heard the story of Christ on the cross, bearing all our sins, and at the invitation he went forward and said, "Preacher, tell me how to be saved." From then on he went about thanking the preacher and praising God, for God had saved him from the pit.
blocks.es_reference: Rescatado del Hoyo: Un joven predicador dirigía un culto de avivamiento cuando una mujer bien vestida bajó por el pasillo y recibió a Cristo. Fue a casa con su esposo, un granjero grande y fornido de más de metro ochenta, y le dijo: "Dave, oí predicar hoy a un joven, y fui salva. Estoy tan feliz — he estado preocupada por dónde pasaría la eternidad, y hoy fui salva." Su esposo la amaba, pero se enfureció tanto que casi la golpeó. "¿Qué clase de hogar vamos a tener," exigió, "contigo salva y yo perdido?" Decidió arreglar cuentas con ese predicador al día siguiente. Vino al culto listo para pelear, y en cambio se quedó sentado manso como un cordero. Oyó la historia de Cristo en la cruz, llevando todos nuestros pecados, y a la invitación pasó al frente y dijo: "Predicador, dígame cómo ser salvo." Desde entonces anduvo dando gracias al predicador y alabando a Dios, porque Dios lo había rescatado del hoyo.

blocks.en: 5. The Fourth Blessing: He Crowns Us with Love and Mercy
blocks.es_reference: 5. La Cuarta Bendición: Él Nos Corona de Amor y Misericordia

blocks.en: The fourth benefit is honor: "who crowns you with lovingkindness and tender mercies." This is no crown of gold, but a crown of steadfast love and mercy. Perhaps David means how close it is — nothing is nearer a person's head than a crown. Perhaps he means how completely it surrounds us, for a crown encircles the head. Whatever the exact picture, the truth is that God's love and mercy are always there, all the way around us, resting on us.
blocks.es_reference: El cuarto beneficio es la honra: "Él es quien te corona de favores y misericordias." No es una corona de oro, sino una corona de amor firme y misericordia. Quizá David se refiere a cuán cerca está — nada está más cerca de la cabeza de una persona que una corona. Quizá se refiere a cuán completamente nos rodea, pues una corona ciñe la cabeza. Sea cual sea la imagen exacta, la verdad es que el amor y la misericordia de Dios siempre están ahí, todo alrededor de nosotros, reposando sobre nosotros.

blocks.en: Nothing can ever cause us to lose that love. Sometimes it feels as though our sin must surely have cost us God's affection, but Jesus promised He would be with us always. As a parent, I know I will never stop loving my children. I may be disappointed with them, I may be angry, I may even have to discipline them — but nothing could make me stop loving them, for my love does not depend on their performance. And it is wonderful beyond words to know that even when I sin, God still crowns me with His love and His mercy. Sometimes it feels as though we have lost that love because He has not answered as we hoped or healed as we asked. But remember that some of God's choicest servants were never healed in this life — the apostle Paul kept his thorn in the flesh, and God told him, "My grace is sufficient for you." The crown of love rests on us still.
blocks.es_reference: Nada puede jamás hacernos perder ese amor. A veces parece que nuestro pecado seguramente nos ha costado el afecto de Dios, pero Jesús prometió que estaría con nosotros siempre. Como padre, sé que nunca dejaré de amar a mis hijos. Puedo decepcionarme de ellos, puedo enojarme, puedo incluso tener que disciplinarlos — pero nada podría hacerme dejar de amarlos, porque mi amor no depende de su desempeño. Y es maravilloso más allá de las palabras saber que aun cuando peco, Dios todavía me corona con Su amor y Su misericordia. A veces parece que hemos perdido ese amor porque Él no respondió como esperábamos ni sanó como pedimos. Pero recuerde que algunos de los siervos más escogidos de Dios nunca fueron sanados en esta vida — el apóstol Pablo conservó su aguijón en la carne, y Dios le dijo: "Bástate mi gracia." La corona de amor reposa sobre nosotros todavía.

blocks.en: 6. The Fifth Blessing: He Satisfies Us with Good
blocks.es_reference: 6. La Quinta Bendición: Él Nos Sacia de Bien

blocks.en: The fifth benefit is provision: "who satisfies your mouth with good things." No human need is finally left unsatisfied by God. He puts food on the table; He clothes the fields; in His providence He cares for the tiniest animal and the most ordinary flower. Surely, then, we can trust Him to care for us. David wrote in another place, "I have been young, and now am old; yet I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his descendants begging bread" — and neither, in all my years, have I.
blocks.es_reference: El quinto beneficio es la provisión: "Él es quien sacia de bien tu boca." Ninguna necesidad humana queda al fin sin satisfacer por Dios. Él pone alimento en la mesa; Él viste los campos; en Su providencia cuida del animal más pequeño y de la flor más común. Seguramente, entonces, podemos confiar en que cuidará de nosotros. David escribió en otro lugar: "Joven fui, y he envejecido, y no he visto justo desamparado, ni su descendencia que mendigue pan" — y tampoco yo, en todos mis años.

blocks.en: Because God gives us our food day by day, we must never take it for granted. A college student once sat down at a cafeteria table with five other girls and quietly bowed her head to say grace. Some of the others laughed. When she finished, she asked why they had laughed. "Aren't you thankful?" she said. "For what?" one replied. "We paid for it." "Where did you get the money?" "From our families." "Where did they get it?" "They worked for it." "And where did they get the strength to work — where did all of it finally come from?" That evening, two more of the girls bowed to say grace before supper; the next day, all six of them did. We bless God because He satisfies our desires with good things.
blocks.es_reference: Porque Dios nos da el alimento día a día, nunca debemos darlo por sentado. Una estudiante universitaria se sentó una vez a una mesa de cafetería con otras cinco muchachas e inclinó en silencio la cabeza para dar gracias. Algunas se rieron. Cuando terminó, preguntó por qué se habían reído. "¿No están agradecidas?" dijo. "¿Por qué?" respondió una. "Nosotras lo pagamos." "¿De dónde sacaron el dinero?" "De nuestras familias." "¿Y de dónde lo sacaron ellas?" "Trabajaron por él." "¿Y de dónde sacaron la fuerza para trabajar — de dónde vino al fin todo?" Esa noche, dos más de las muchachas inclinaron la cabeza para dar gracias antes de la cena; al día siguiente, las seis lo hicieron. Bendecimos a Dios porque sacia de bien nuestros deseos.

blocks.en: 7. The Sixth Blessing: He Renews Our Strength
blocks.es_reference: 7. La Sexta Bendición: Él Renueva Nuestras Fuerzas

blocks.en: Psalm 103:5 (NKJV): "…so that your youth is renewed like the eagle's."
blocks.es_reference: Salmo 103:5 (RVG): "…de modo que te rejuvenezcas como el águila."

blocks.en: The sixth benefit is renewal: our youth renewed like the eagle's. One of the deepest longings of the human heart is to stay young; billions are spent every year on cosmetics and surgery and exercise to turn back the clock. Ponce de León was neither the first nor the last to search for the fountain of youth. But sooner or later time wears down every earthly body. The renewal David sings of is something else entirely. As Isaiah promised, "those who wait on the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings like eagles; they shall run and not be weary; they shall walk and not faint." That kind of renewal has nothing to do with age. I have known young people with no reason to live and no purpose, and I have known saints in their seventies and eighties and nineties who were soaring with the eagles — a zest for life, a zest for witnessing, a zest for God. Where do they get such strength? They are renewed continually by God Himself.
blocks.es_reference: El sexto beneficio es la renovación: nuestra juventud renovada como la del águila. Uno de los anhelos más profundos del corazón humano es seguir joven; se gastan miles de millones cada año en cosméticos, cirugías y ejercicio para hacer retroceder el reloj. Ponce de León no fue ni el primero ni el último en buscar la fuente de la juventud. Pero tarde o temprano el tiempo desgasta todo cuerpo terrenal. La renovación que David canta es algo enteramente distinto. Como prometió Isaías: "los que esperan a Jehová tendrán nuevas fuerzas; levantarán las alas como águilas; correrán, y no se cansarán; caminarán, y no se fatigarán." Esa clase de renovación no tiene nada que ver con la edad. He conocido jóvenes sin razón para vivir y sin propósito, y he conocido santos de setenta, ochenta y noventa años que volaban con las águilas — con ánimo para vivir, ánimo para testificar, ánimo para Dios. ¿De dónde sacan tal fuerza? Son renovados continuamente por Dios mismo.

blocks.en: 8. Telling It with Our Last Breath
blocks.es_reference: 8. Contándolo con Nuestro Último Aliento

blocks.en: John Jasper's Joy: When John Jasper, the great preacher who had been a slave, was converted, his master told him, "Keep telling it, John. Fly like an angel, and wherever you go, tell it!" Jasper said of his conversion morning: "O happy day! Can I ever forget it? That was my conversion morning, and that was the day the Lord sent me out with the good news of the kingdom. For more than sixty years I've been telling it. My step is getting rather slow, my voice breaks down, and sometimes I'm awful tired. But still I'm telling it. My lips shall sing the dying love of the Lamb with my last expiring breath." That is what a counted blessing finally becomes — not a private comfort hoarded up, but a song that must be sung, a testimony that must be told.
blocks.es_reference: El Gozo de John Jasper: Cuando John Jasper, el gran predicador que había sido esclavo, se convirtió, su amo le dijo: "Sigue contándolo, John. Vuela como un ángel, y dondequiera que vayas, ¡cuéntalo!" Jasper dijo de la mañana de su conversión: "¡Oh día feliz! ¿Podré olvidarlo alguna vez? Esa fue la mañana de mi conversión, y ese fue el día en que el Señor me envió con las buenas nuevas del reino. Por más de sesenta años lo he estado contando. Mi paso se hace algo lento, mi voz se quiebra, y a veces estoy terriblemente cansado. Pero todavía lo cuento. Mis labios cantarán el amor agonizante del Cordero con mi último aliento." En eso se convierte al fin una bendición contada — no en un consuelo privado guardado para uno mismo, sino en una canción que debe cantarse, un testimonio que debe contarse.

blocks.en: So David gathers up all the benefits of God — forgiveness, healing, rescue from the pit, the crown of love, satisfaction with good, and renewed strength — and ties them into one great song of praise. Thank God that He renews our strength through Jesus Christ, and gives us a youth that the world and the years can never touch. Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all His benefits. Count them, name them one by one, and it will surprise you what the Lord has done.
blocks.es_reference: Así David reúne todos los beneficios de Dios — el perdón, la sanidad, el rescate del hoyo, la corona de amor, la satisfacción con el bien, y las fuerzas renovadas — y los ata en una gran canción de alabanza. Gracias a Dios que renueva nuestras fuerzas por medio de Jesucristo, y nos da una juventud que el mundo y los años nunca pueden tocar. Bendice, alma mía, a Jehová, y no olvides ninguno de sus beneficios. Cuéntalos, nómbralos uno a uno, y verás, sorprendido, lo que el Señor ha hecho.

mc.stem: The paralyzed man who asked for "Count Your Blessings" at the revival illustrates what attitude the lesson commends?
options: Gratitude that counts God's mercies even in the midst of suffering
That the sick should be left alone
That cheerful people are never truly ill
mc.why: The paralyzed man who asked for 'Count Your Blessings' models gratitude that counts God's mercies even in suffering.

mc.stem: According to the lesson, why did David have to "tie his blessings into bundles"?
options: He was running out of time
There were so many he needed to group them to remember them all
He could only count to ten
mc.why: David had so many blessings he tied them into bundles to remember them all — God's benefits are beyond counting.

mc.stem: To what does the lesson compare ungrateful, complaining Christians?
options: Starving men hired to carry signs for the finest restaurant
mc.why: Ungrateful, complaining Christians are like starving men carrying signs for the finest restaurant — they advertise what they won't enjoy.

mc.stem: What does Psalm 103:2 call us to do?
options: Fear the Lord and depart from evil
Sing a new song to the Lord
Bless the Lord and forget not all His benefits
mc.why: Psalm 103:2 sets the theme: 'Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all His benefits.'

mc.stem: What is the FIRST benefit David names in Psalm 103?
mc.why: The first benefit David names is forgiveness — God forgives all our iniquities, the deepest mercy of all.

mc.stem: How does the lesson describe sin throughout the Bible?
options: As a disease that is always fatal, which every person carries
As a debt that can be repaid
As a problem only for some people
mc.why: Throughout the Bible sin is pictured as a disease that is always fatal, and which every person carries.

mc.stem: In illustrating forgiveness, the lesson recalls the woman about to be stoned. What did Jesus say to her?
options: "Neither do I condemn you; go and sin no more"
"Today you will be with Me in paradise"
mc.why: To the woman about to be stoned Jesus said, 'Neither do I condemn you; go and sin no more' — forgiveness with a call to new life.

mc.stem: What is the SECOND benefit David names?
mc.why: The second benefit is healing — He heals all our diseases, in His time and way.

mc.stem: What does the lesson conclude about the source of all healing?
options: All healing is finally divine healing and a gift from God
Healing is purely a matter of willpower
mc.why: Whether through a doctor's hands or direct mercy, all healing is finally divine healing and a gift from God.

mc.stem: Which Gospel account does the lesson use to illustrate God's healing?
options: The woman with the issue of blood who touched His garment
The man at the pool of Bethesda
mc.why: The woman with the issue of blood touched His garment and was healed — picturing healing that comes by faith in Christ.

mc.stem: What is the THIRD benefit, and what does "the pit" refer to?
options: Redemption from the pit; the grave and the eternal pit of hell
Strength; the weakness of old age
mc.why: The third benefit is redemption from the pit — both the grave and the eternal pit of hell, from which Christ saves us.

mc.stem: In the "saved from the pit" story, how did the furious farmer respond after coming to the service?
options: He waited silently and left unchanged
He went forward and asked how to be saved
mc.why: The furious farmer came to fight the preacher but, hearing of the cross, went forward and asked how to be saved.

mc.stem: What is the FOURTH benefit David names?
options: He crowns us with lovingkindness and tender mercies
He gives us a crown of gold
He makes us rulers over nations
mc.why: The fourth benefit is honor — He crowns us with lovingkindness and tender mercies that surround us completely.

mc.stem: What does the lesson say about whether our sin can cause us to lose God's love?
options: Nothing can cause us to lose it; His love does not depend on our performance
We must earn His love back each day
Only great sins forfeit His love
mc.why: Nothing can make us lose God's love; like a parent's love, it does not depend on our performance.

mc.stem: Which example shows that some of God's choicest servants were not healed in this life?
options: Paul keeping his thorn in the flesh, told 'My grace is sufficient'
mc.why: Paul kept his thorn in the flesh and was told 'My grace is sufficient' — God's choicest servants are not always healed here.

mc.stem: What is the FIFTH benefit David names?
options: He satisfies our mouth with good things
mc.why: The fifth benefit is provision — He satisfies our mouth with good things; no true need is left unmet.

mc.stem: The cafeteria story, where the girls said "we paid for it," is used to teach what about our daily provision?
options: That ultimately every good thing traces back to God, who deserves our thanks
That paying for food removes the need for prayer
That gratitude is only for special occasions
mc.why: The cafeteria story teaches that ultimately every good thing traces back to God, who deserves our thanks.

mc.stem: What is the SIXTH benefit, pictured as "renewed like the eagle's"?
options: Renewal of our strength and youth
mc.why: The sixth benefit is renewal — our strength and youth renewed like the eagle's, a vigor the years cannot touch.

mc.stem: According to the lesson, the renewal David sings of has nothing to do with what?
mc.why: This renewal has nothing to do with age; saints in their nineties can soar while the young may have no life at all.

mc.stem: In the closing illustration, what did John Jasper vow to do with his last expiring breath?
options: Rest at last from his labors
Sing the dying love of the Lamb — keep telling it
mc.why: John Jasper vowed to sing the dying love of the Lamb with his last breath — a counted blessing becomes a testimony to tell.

sa.prompt: Explain the opening illustration of the paralyzed man and the hymn, and how it sets up the theme of Psalm 103.
sa.model: The lesson opens with a paralyzed man at a revival who, unable to do anything else, called for the hymn "Count Your Blessings." Even in his affliction he chose gratitude, numbering God's mercies rather than his troubles. This sets up the theme of Psalm 103, which is one long call to bless the LORD and forget not all His benefits. The man becomes a living picture of what the psalm teaches: that thankfulness is not a response to easy circumstances but a deliberate counting of God's goodness in every condition, even hardship. Psalm 103 trains the soul to do exactly that.

sa.prompt: Why does the lesson say David had to "tie his blessings into bundles," and what attitude does Psalm 103 call us to?
sa.model: The lesson says David had so many blessings that he had to "tie them into bundles" to take them in, grouping God's benefits because they were too many to count one by one. Psalm 103 then calls us to the same practice: "Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all His benefits." The attitude the psalm calls for is deliberate, grateful remembering. Our natural tendency is to forget mercies and dwell on complaints; David disciplines his soul to do the opposite, to recall and rehearse God's goodness. Gratitude here is not a mood but a chosen act of remembering what God has done.

sa.prompt: Explain the first benefit, forgiveness, including how the lesson pictures sin and its only cure.
sa.model: The first benefit David names is forgiveness: God "forgives all your iniquities." The lesson pictures sin as a disease that is always fatal and which every person carries; left untreated it ends in eternal death. The only cure is the forgiveness God provides through the cross of Christ, where our sin was paid for. When God forgives, He deals with the deepest problem we have, not merely our circumstances but our guilt. This is named first because it is the greatest benefit of all: every other mercy flows from being a forgiven people, restored to the God against whom we had sinned.

sa.prompt: Explain the second benefit, healing, and use the woman with the issue of blood to show the source of healing.
sa.model: The second benefit is that God "heals all your diseases." The woman with the issue of blood, who had spent all she had on physicians without help, touched the hem of Jesus' garment in faith and was healed. The lesson uses her to show the true source of healing: it comes from God, received by faith in Christ. Whether God heals through a physician's skill or by direct mercy, all healing is finally His gift. He cares about the body as well as the soul. Yet the deepest healing is the wholeness He gives His people, in His time and way, for our good.

sa.prompt: Explain the third benefit, redemption from the pit, including both meanings of "the pit."
sa.model: The third benefit is that God "redeems your life from the pit." The lesson explains that "the pit" carries two meanings. It refers to the grave, the physical death from which God will finally raise His people; and it refers to the eternal pit, hell itself, from which Christ redeems all who trust Him. To redeem is to buy back at a price, and the price was the blood of Christ. So this benefit reaches past our present troubles to our ultimate destiny: God has rescued us from both the grave's final hold and the eternal ruin our sin deserved, securing us forever.

sa.prompt: What does the account of the farmer who was "saved from the pit" illustrate about God's power to redeem a hardened heart?
sa.model: The lesson tells of a furious farmer who came to a service angry, perhaps intending to cause trouble, but who, on hearing the message of the cross, was so moved that he went forward and asked how to be saved. The account illustrates God's power to redeem even a hardened heart. No one is beyond the reach of grace; the very man who arrived in anger left as a new creation. It shows that the gospel does not depend on the worthiness or readiness of the hearer but on the power of God to break through and rescue, lifting a soul out of the pit of sin.

sa.prompt: Explain the fourth benefit, the crown of love and mercy, and why we cannot lose God's love.
sa.model: The fourth benefit is that God "crowns you with lovingkindness and tender mercies." To be crowned is to be surrounded and honored; God encircles His people with steadfast love and compassion. The lesson stresses that we cannot lose this love by our failures, because it does not depend on our performance but on God's own faithful character, like a parent's love for a child. Our sin grieves Him, but it cannot make Him stop loving us. This is profound security: the believer lives crowned with a love that was never earned and therefore can never be lost through unworthiness.

sa.prompt: Explain the fifth benefit, satisfaction with good, and use the cafeteria grace story.
sa.model: The fifth benefit is that God "satisfies your mouth with good things." He is a generous provider who meets the real needs of His people. The cafeteria grace story shows the wrong attitude: some girls would not give thanks, their first reason being "we paid for it." But the lesson points out that ultimately every good thing traces back to God, the money, the work, the food, the very life that earned it. Nothing we have is finally self-made. Recognizing that all good comes from God turns ordinary provision into an occasion for gratitude, and guards us from the pride that forgets the Giver.

sa.prompt: Explain the sixth benefit, renewal of strength, and how Isaiah's eagle promise differs from the world's search for youth.
sa.model: The sixth benefit is that God renews our strength, so that our "youth is renewed like the eagle's." The lesson is careful to say this renewal has nothing to do with age; it is not about staying physically young. It is the inner renewal Isaiah promised: those who wait on the LORD renew their strength and mount up with wings like eagles. The world spends itself searching for youth in the body and always loses the race; God gives a renewal of spirit that the years cannot touch. Saints can grow stronger in faith as the body weakens, soaring on a vigor that comes from waiting on the Lord.

sa.prompt: Retell John Jasper's testimony and explain what a counted blessing should finally become.
sa.model: John Jasper, a former slave who became a powerful preacher, vowed that with his last expiring breath he would keep singing the dying love of the Lamb, telling of Christ to the very end. The lesson uses him to show what a counted blessing should finally become: not a private comfort hoarded for ourselves, but a testimony we tell to others. When we have truly numbered God's benefits, forgiveness, healing, redemption, love, satisfaction, renewal, the natural overflow is praise that proclaims His goodness. The blessings we count are meant to be turned outward, becoming the song and witness of a grateful life until our final breath.
